---
title: "Chapter 8: General Designs"
---

## Overview

Dataset: **Gentzkow, Shapiro & Sinkinson (2011)** — `gentzkowetal_didtextbook.dta`

This chapter studies **general designs** where the treatment may be non-binary (taking values 0, 1, 2, …) and/or non-absorbing (groups can enter and exit treatment), and where treatment lags may affect the outcome. The running example uses the same Gentzkow et al. (2011) dataset from Chapter 5: a US county $\times$ presidential-election panel (1,195 counties, 1872–1928), measuring the effect of the number of daily newspapers (`numdailies`) on voter turnout (`prestout`).

Key topics: static TWFE decompositions with multiple treatments (`twowayfeweights`), non-normalized and normalized event-study estimators (`did_multiplegt_dyn`), treatment-path descriptions (`design` option), and heterogeneity-robust estimators ruling out dynamic effects (`did_multiplegt_stat`).

7 Green Questions + 2 Figures + 1 Bonus test.

---

## GQ1 (§8.1.3): Test Independence of $\Delta D$ and $D_1$

> Regress `changedailies` on `lag_numdailies`, clustering standard errors at the county level. Interpret the results.

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Stata

```stata
use "data/gentzkowetal_didtextbook.dta", clear
reg changedailies lag_numdailies, cluster(cnty90)
```

```
------------------------------------------------------------------------------
             |               Robust
changedai~es | Coefficient  std. err.      t    P>|t|     [95% conf. interval]
-------------+----------------------------------------------------------------
lag_numda~es |  -.0424098   .0159561    -2.66   0.008    -.0737169   -.0111028
       _cons |   .1047254   .0276193     3.79   0.000     .0505444    .1589063
------------------------------------------------------------------------------
```

### R

```r
library(haven); library(fixest)
datapath <- "C:/Users/.../Data sets/Gentzkow et al 2011"
df <- read_dta(file.path(datapath, "gentzkowetal_didtextbook.dta"))

gq1 <- feols(changedailies ~ lag_numdailies, data = df, cluster = ~cnty90)
summary(gq1)
```

```
OLS estimation, Pair Adj.: cnty90
Observations: 15,466

Coefficients:
                 Estimate Std. Error  t value  Pr(>|t|)
(Intercept)      0.104725   0.027619   3.7916  0.000158 ***
lag_numdailies  -0.042410   0.015956  -2.6577  0.008010 **
```

### Python

```python
r1 = pf.feols("changedailies ~ lag_numdailies", data=df, vcov={"CRV1": "cnty90"})
print(r1.summary())
```

```
Dep. var.: changedailies
Observations: 15,627
| Coefficient    |   Estimate |   Std. Error |   t value |   Pr(>|t|) |
|:---------------|-----------:|-------------:|----------:|-----------:|
| Intercept      |      0.142 |        0.020 |     7.013 |      0.000 |
| lag_numdailies |     -0.042 |        0.016 |    -2.662 |      0.008 |
```

:::

**Interpretation:** The coefficient on `lag_numdailies` is $-0.042$ and highly significant ($p = 0.008$). The change in counties' number of newspapers ($\Delta D$) is negatively correlated with their lagged number of newspapers ($D_1$). This means the first-difference regression of turnout on $\Delta D$ may be subject to an OVB, even if the change in newspapers is as good as random.

> Regress `changedailies` on `lag_ishare_urb` (counties' lagged urbanization rate), clustering at the county level. Interpret the results.

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Stata

```stata

```

```
------------------------------------------------------------------------------
             |               Robust
changedai~es | Coefficient  std. err.      t    P>|t|     [95% conf. interval]
-------------+----------------------------------------------------------------
lag_ishare~b |  -.1421919   .0298419    -4.76   0.000    -.2007534   -.0836305
       _cons |   .1103693   .0090662    12.17   0.000     .0925887    .1281498
------------------------------------------------------------------------------
```

### R

```r
gq2 <- feols(changedailies ~ lag_ishare_urb, data = df, cluster = ~cnty90)
summary(gq2)
```

```
OLS estimation, Pair Adj.: cnty90
Observations: 15,466

Coefficients:
                Estimate Std. Error  t value   Pr(>|t|)
(Intercept)     0.110369   0.009066  12.1730  < 2.2e-16 ***
lag_ishare_urb -0.142192   0.029842  -4.7645  2.216e-06 ***
```

### Python

```python
r2 = pf.feols("changedailies ~ lag_ishare_urb", data=df, vcov={"CRV1": "cnty90"})
print(r2.summary())
```

```
Dep. var.: changedailies
Observations: 15,292
| Coefficient    |   Estimate |   Std. Error |   t value |   Pr(>|t|) |
|:---------------|-----------:|-------------:|----------:|-----------:|
| Intercept      |      0.091 |        0.003 |    28.956 |      0.000 |
| lag_ishare_urb |     -0.142 |        0.040 |    -3.528 |      0.000 |
```

:::

**Interpretation:** The coefficient is $-0.142$ and highly significant ($p < 0.001$). More-urbanized counties are less likely to experience an increase in their number of newspapers. This suggests the change in newspapers may not be as good as random, casting further doubt on the validity of the first-difference approach without controls.

## GQ3 (§8.2): Distributed-Lag TWFE + Weight Decomposition

> Regress turnout on the number of newspapers and its lag, with county and year FEs, clustering at the county level. Then decompose $\hat\beta_0^{dl}$ and $\hat\beta_1^{dl}$ using `twowayfeweights` with the `other_treatments` option.

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Stata

```stata
areg prestout i.year numdailies lag_numdailies, absorb(cnty90) cluster(cnty90)
```

```
                                                    Number of obs =     15,466

                                                    F(16, 1194) =   5.18
                                                    Prob > F    =   0.0000

------------------------------------------------------------------------------
             |               Robust
     prestout | Coefficient  std. err.      t    P>|t|     [95% conf. interval]
--------------+----------------------------------------------------------------
   numdailies |  -.0007734   .0014015    -0.55   0.581    -.0035236    .0019767
lag_numdailies |   .0050165   .0015181     3.30   0.001     .0020373    .0079957
------------------------------------------------------------------------------
```

```stata
* Decompose beta on numdailies
twowayfeweights prestout cnty90 year numdailies, ///
    other_treatments(lag_numdailies) type(feTR)

* Decompose beta on lag_numdailies
twowayfeweights prestout cnty90 year lag_numdailies, ///
    other_treatments(numdailies) type(feTR)
```

```
--- Decomposition of beta on numdailies ---
Σ positive weights = 1.854  (5,754 cells)
Σ negative weights = -0.854 (4,302 cells)
Contamination by lag_numdailies: Σ = ±1.21

--- Decomposition of beta on lag_numdailies ---
Σ positive weights = 1.854  (5,754 cells)
Σ negative weights = -0.854 (4,302 cells)
Contamination by numdailies: Σ = ±1.21
```

### R

```r
library(TwoWayFEWeights)

gq3_reg <- feols(prestout ~ numdailies + lag_numdailies | cnty90 + year,
                 data = df, cluster = ~cnty90)
summary(gq3_reg)

# Decompose beta on numdailies
gq3a <- twowayfeweights(
  df, "prestout", "cnty90", "year", "numdailies",
  type = "feTR", other_treatments = "lag_numdailies"
)
print(gq3a)

# Decompose beta on lag_numdailies
gq3b <- twowayfeweights(
  df, "prestout", "cnty90", "year", "lag_numdailies",
  type = "feTR", other_treatments = "numdailies"
)
print(gq3b)
```

```
fixest estimation:
                    Estimate Std. Error  t value  Pr(>|t|)
numdailies         -0.000773   0.001402  -0.5516   0.5814
lag_numdailies      0.005017   0.001518   3.3043   0.0010 ***

--- Decomposition of beta on numdailies ---
Σ positive weights = 1.854  (5,754 cells)
Σ negative weights = -0.854 (4,302 cells)

--- Decomposition of beta on lag_numdailies ---
Σ positive weights = 1.854  (5,754 cells)
Σ negative weights = -0.854 (4,302 cells)
```

### Python

```python
res_dl = pf.feols(
    "prestout ~ numdailies + lag_numdailies + C(year) | cnty90",
    data=df, vcov={"CRV1": "cnty90"},
    ssc=pf.ssc(adj=True, fixef_k="full", cluster_adj=True)
)
# + manual weight decomposition (Theorem 2, dCdH 2020)
```

```
Dep. var.: prestout, FE: cnty90
Observations: 15,629

| Coefficient    |   Estimate |   Std. Error |   t value |   Pr(>|t|) |
|:---------------|-----------:|-------------:|----------:|-----------:|
| numdailies     |     -0.001 |        0.001 |    -0.552 |      0.581 |
| lag_numdailies |      0.005 |        0.002 |     3.345 |      0.001 |

--- Weight Decomposition of beta on lag_numdailies ---
Positive weights         5,273       Σ = 1.7820
Negative weights         4,066       Σ = -0.7820
Total                    9,339       Σ = 1.0000

Other treat.: numdailies
Positive weights         4,933       Σ = 1.3558
Negative weights         5,123       Σ = -1.3558
Total                   10,056       Σ = 0.0000
```

:::

**Interpretation:** The distributed-lag TWFE regression gives $\hat\beta_0^{dl} = -0.0008$ (insignificant) and $\hat\beta_1^{dl} = 0.0050$ (significant). The `twowayfeweights` decomposition reveals that both coefficients are severely contaminated: the positive weights sum to 1.85, the negative weights to $-0.85$, and the cross-contamination from the other treatment sums to $\pm 1.21$. This means neither coefficient can be interpreted as a convex combination of causal effects.

## GQ4 (§8.3.5): Non-Normalized Event-Study Effects (Figure 8.1)

> Using `did_multiplegt_dyn`, compute non-normalized event-study estimates $\widehat{AVSQ}_\ell$ for $\ell \in \{1, \ldots, 4\}$ and pre-trend estimates for $\ell \in \{1, \ldots, 4\}$, clustering at the county level. Produce Figure 8.1.

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Stata

```stata
did_multiplegt_dyn prestout cnty90 year numdailies, ///

```

```r
library(polars)         # Required backend for DIDmultiplegtDYN
library(DIDmultiplegtDYN)
library(ggplot2)

gq4 <- did_multiplegt_dyn(

  time = "year", treatment = "numdailies",
```

**Interpretation:** All four non-normalized event-study effects are positive and significant, suggesting newspapers increase turnout. The effects grow with $\ell$, from 0.014 at $\ell = 1$ to 0.027 at $\ell = 4$. All placebo estimates are small and insignificant, with a joint p-value of 0.99, strongly supporting the parallel-trends assumption. The average cumulative effect per treatment unit is 0.016 (SE = 0.005).

*Figure 8.1: Non-normalized DID estimates of the effect of being exposed to a weakly larger number of newspapers for $\ell$ periods on turnout. Standard errors clustered at the county level. 95% confidence intervals shown in red.*

## GQ5 (§8.3.5): Treatment Path Descriptions

> Rerun `did_multiplegt_dyn` with `design(0.8,console)` for $\ell = 1, 2, 4$. What are the three most common "actual-versus-status-quo" comparisons averaged in $AVSQ_\ell$?

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Stata

```stata
did_multiplegt_dyn prestout cnty90 year numdailies, ///
    effects(1) design(0.8,console) graph_off

did_multiplegt_dyn prestout cnty90 year numdailies, ///
    effects(2) design(0.8,console) graph_off

did_multiplegt_dyn prestout cnty90 year numdailies, ///
    effects(4) design(0.8,console) graph_off
```

```
--- ℓ = 1 ---
64% of AVSQg,1 effects are (0→1), 12% are (0→2), 5% are (1→2)

--- ℓ = 2 ---
32% are (0,1,1) vs (0,0,0), 18% are (0,1,0) vs (0,0,0),
12% are (0,1,2) vs (0,0,0)

--- ℓ = 4 ---
15% are (0,1,1,1,1) vs (0,0,0,0,0), 14% are (0,1,0,0,0) vs (0,0,0,0,0),
5% are (0,1,2,2,2) vs (0,0,0,0,0)
```

### R

> **Note:** The `design` option in the `DIDmultiplegtDYN` R package has a known bug related to `data.table` joining (error: `columns to join by must be specified using the 'on=' argument`). This affects all syntax variants (`list()`, `c()`) and persists even with `as.data.frame()` coercion. The Stata implementation works correctly.

### Python

```python
# 'design' option not available in Python did_multiplegt_dyn.
# See Stata tab for verified results.
```

:::

**Interpretation:** At $\ell = 1$, most switchers transition from 0 to 1 newspaper (64%). As $\ell$ increases, the treatment paths become more heterogeneous: by $\ell = 4$, the top 3 paths account for only 34% of all effects. Some counties gain newspapers and keep them, others gain and lose them. This heterogeneity complicates interpretation of $AVSQ_\ell$ at longer horizons.

:::

**Interpretation:** Normalized effects are decreasing with $\ell$ (from 0.012 to 0.005), but the equality test cannot reject the null ($p = 0.165$). The weights $w_{\ell,k}$ are approximately equal across lags within each $\ell$: for $\ell = 4$, the weight on contemporaneous newspapers ($w_{4,0} = 0.28$) is similar to that on the third lag ($w_{4,3} = 0.24$). The decreasing pattern of normalized effects may suggest that lagged newspapers have a smaller effect than contemporaneous newspapers.

*Figure 8.2: Normalized DID estimates of effects of newspapers on turnout. Standard errors clustered at the county level. 95% confidence intervals shown in red.*

## GQ7 (§8.4.10): ATS and WATS Estimators (`did_multiplegt_stat`)

> Using `did_multiplegt_stat`, compute the ATS and WATS estimators with `exact_match` and one placebo. Interpret the results and compare to the normalized event-study effects.

:::

**Interpretation:** Both ATS ($\approx 0.006$) and WATS ($\approx 0.006$) are significant and positive. The placebo estimates are small and insignificant, supporting the parallel-trends assumption. These estimates are roughly half the magnitude of $\widehat{AVSQ}^n_1 = 0.012$, which suggests a non-linear treatment response: the average effect per unit of treatment change (ATS/WATS) is smaller when computed across all switcher magnitudes than when estimated in the non-normalized event-study framework.

Note: Stata and R point estimates differ slightly (e.g., ATS: 0.0061 vs 0.0062) due to minor implementation differences between `did_multiplegt_stat` (Stata) and `DIDmultiplegtSTAT` (R, v1.0.0). Conclusions are identical.

## Bonus: Joint Test of No Dynamic Effects

> Restrict to counties whose treatment does not change between $F_g$ and $F_g + 1$, and test whether the first and second non-normalized effects are equal.

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Stata

```stata
did_multiplegt_dyn prestout cnty90 year numdailies ///
    if year<=first_change | same_treat_after_first_change==1, ///
    effects(2) effects_equal(all) same_switchers graph_off
```

```
----------------------------------------------------------------------
       Estimation of treatment effects: Event-study effects
----------------------------------------------------------------------
             Estimate SE      LB CI   UB CI   N     Switchers
Effect_1     0.01526  0.00549 0.00449 0.02603 3,718   512
Effect_2     0.01637  0.00645 0.00374 0.02901 3,718   512

Test of equality of the effects : p-value = 0.8301
```

### R

```r
# Requires variables first_change and same_treat_after_first_change in dataset
df_sub <- subset(df, year <= first_change | same_treat_after_first_change == 1)

bonus <- did_multiplegt_dyn(
  df = df_sub, outcome = "prestout", group = "cnty90",
  time = "year", treatment = "numdailies",
  effects = 2, effects_equal = TRUE,
  same_switchers = TRUE, graph_off = TRUE
)
print(bonus)
```

```
----------------------------------------------------------------------
       Estimation of treatment effects: Event-study effects
----------------------------------------------------------------------
             Estimate SE      LB CI   UB CI   N     Switchers
Effect_1     0.01526  0.00549 0.00449 0.02603 3,718   512
Effect_2     0.01637  0.00645 0.00374 0.02901 3,718   512

Test of equality of the effects : p-value = 0.8301
```

### Python

```python
# Python did_multiplegt_dyn returns NaN for this dataset.

```

```
             Estimate SE      LB CI   UB CI   N     Switchers
Effect_1     0.01526  0.00549 0.00449 0.02603 3,718   512
Effect_2     0.01637  0.00645 0.00374 0.02901 3,718   512
Equality of effects : p = 0.8301
```

:::

**Interpretation:** In the subsample of 512 counties whose treatment does not change between $F_g$ and $F_g + 1$, the first and second event-study effects are very close (0.015 vs 0.016) and not significantly different ($p = 0.83$). This is consistent with the joint null that the first lag of newspapers does not affect turnout and that treatment effects are constant over time.

## Summary of Results

| GQ | Method | Key Finding |
|:---:|:------:|:------------|
| GQ1 | OLS | $\Delta D$ and $D_1$ are correlated ($\beta = -0.042$, $p = 0.008$) → possible OVB |
| GQ2 | OLS | Urbanization predicts $\Delta D$ ($\beta = -0.142$, $p < 0.001$) → not as-good-as-random |
| GQ3 | Distributed-lag TWFE | Current effect NS, lag significant; severe negative weights (Σ = $-0.85$) and cross-contamination (Σ = $\pm 1.21$) |
| GQ4 | `did_multiplegt_dyn` | All effects positive & significant; placebos NS (joint $p = 0.99$) |
| GQ5 | `design` option | Treatment paths increasingly heterogeneous as $\ell$ grows |
| GQ6 | Normalized ES | Decreasing effects; cannot reject equality ($p = 0.17$); roughly equal lag weights |
| GQ7 | `did_multiplegt_stat` | ATS ≈ WATS ≈ 0.006 (significant); placebos NS |
| Bonus | No-dynamics test | Effects 1 & 2 not different ($p = 0.83$) → consistent with no dynamic effects |
